results.name: two_example_dip
results.description: Yes rate (non-example targets) on 2-example sets minus the mean of the yes rates on 3- and 4-example sets; observed below null means people are more conservative after two examples, relative to larger sets, than the model's monotone capacity limit predicts.
results.code:
# name: two_example_dip
# description: Yes rate (non-example targets) on 2-example sets minus the mean of the yes rates on 3- and 4-example sets; observed below null means people are more conservative after two examples, relative to larger sets, than the model's monotone capacity limit predicts.
def test_statistic(df):
    E = df["number_set"].astype(str).str.split(",", expand=True).apply(pd.to_numeric, errors="coerce").to_numpy(float)
    t = df["target"].astype(int).to_numpy()
    y = df["rating"].astype(float).to_numpy()
    pad = np.isnan(E)
    n = (~pad).sum(axis=1)
    in_set = (E == t[:, None]).any(axis=1)
    def rate(mask):
        return float(y[mask].mean()) if mask.any() else 0.0
    base = ~in_set
    return rate(base & (n == 2)) - 0.5 * (rate(base & (n == 3)) + rate(base & (n == 4)))

results.name: pure_parity_opposite_parity_yes
results.description: In sets of >=2 examples that are all odd or all even, yes rate for targets of the opposite parity; observed below null means people exclude parity-violating targets more strictly than the model predicts (model over-generalizes across parity).
results.code:
# name: pure_parity_opposite_parity_yes
# description: In sets of >=2 examples that are all odd or all even, yes rate for targets of the opposite parity; observed below null means people exclude parity-violating targets more strictly than the model predicts (model over-generalizes across parity).
def test_statistic(df):
    E = df["number_set"].astype(str).str.split(",", expand=True).apply(pd.to_numeric, errors="coerce").to_numpy(float)
    t = df["target"].astype(int).to_numpy()
    y = df["rating"].astype(float).to_numpy()
    pad = np.isnan(E)
    n = (~pad).sum(axis=1)
    in_set = (E == t[:, None]).any(axis=1)
    def rate(mask):
        return float(y[mask].mean()) if mask.any() else 0.0
    all_odd = ((E % 2 == 1) | pad).all(axis=1)
    all_even = ((E % 2 == 0) | pad).all(axis=1)
    opp = (all_odd & (t % 2 == 0)) | (all_even & (t % 2 == 1))
    return rate((n >= 2) & opp)

results.name: square_power_rule_target_yes
results.description: In sets of >=2 examples that are all perfect squares or all powers of 2, yes rate for non-example targets belonging to that same rule; observed below null means people endorse square/power-of-2 rule members less than the model predicts (model over-commits to these rules), above means more.
results.code:
# name: square_power_rule_target_yes
# description: In sets of >=2 examples that are all perfect squares or all powers of 2, yes rate for non-example targets belonging to that same rule; observed below null means people endorse square/power-of-2 rule members less than the model predicts (model over-commits to these rules), above means more.
def test_statistic(df):
    E = df["number_set"].astype(str).str.split(",", expand=True).apply(pd.to_numeric, errors="coerce").to_numpy(float)
    t = df["target"].astype(int).to_numpy()
    y = df["rating"].astype(float).to_numpy()
    pad = np.isnan(E)
    n = (~pad).sum(axis=1)
    in_set = (E == t[:, None]).any(axis=1)
    def rate(mask):
        return float(y[mask].mean()) if mask.any() else 0.0
    sq = np.array([k * k for k in range(1, 11)], dtype=float)
    p2 = np.array([2 ** k for k in range(0, 7)], dtype=float)
    all_sq = (np.isin(E, sq) | pad).all(axis=1) & (n >= 2)
    all_p2 = (np.isin(E, p2) | pad).all(axis=1) & (n >= 2)
    member = (all_sq & np.isin(t, sq)) | (all_p2 & np.isin(t, p2))
    return rate(member & ~in_set)

results.description: Yes rate on trials whose target is itself one of the shown examples; observed below null means people say no to shown examples (lapses/guessing) more than the model, which nearly always endorses them, predicts.

results.name: multiples_of_five_set_gap
results.description: In sets of >=2 examples that are all multiples of 5, yes rate for non-example multiples of 5 minus yes rate for non-multiples; observed below null means people generalize such sets to all multiples of 5 less than the split-out multiples-of-5 prior predicts, above means more.
results.code:
# name: multiples_of_five_set_gap
# description: In sets of >=2 examples that are all multiples of 5, yes rate for non-example multiples of 5 minus yes rate for non-multiples; observed below null means people generalize such sets to all multiples of 5 less than the split-out multiples-of-5 prior predicts, above means more.
def test_statistic(df):
    E = df["number_set"].astype(str).str.split(",", expand=True).apply(pd.to_numeric, errors="coerce").to_numpy(float)
    t = df["target"].astype(int).to_numpy()
    y = df["rating"].astype(float).to_numpy()
    pad = np.isnan(E)
    n = (~pad).sum(axis=1)
    in_set = (E == t[:, None]).any(axis=1)
    def rate(mask):
        return float(y[mask].mean()) if mask.any() else 0.0
    all_five = ((E % 5 == 0) | pad).all(axis=1) & (n >= 2)
    base = all_five & ~in_set
    return rate(base & (t % 5 == 0)) - rate(base & (t % 5 != 0))

results.name: unfamiliar_multiple_rule_gap
results.description: In sets of >=2 examples, not all even and not all multiples of 5, whose examples are all multiples of some m in {3,7,9,11} (largest such m), yes rate for non-example multiples of m minus non-multiples; observed below null means people generalize by unfamiliar multiples rules less than the model predicts, above means more.
results.code:
# name: unfamiliar_multiple_rule_gap
# description: In sets of >=2 examples, not all even and not all multiples of 5, whose examples are all multiples of some m in {3,7,9,11} (largest such m), yes rate for non-example multiples of m minus non-multiples; observed below null means people generalize by unfamiliar multiples rules less than the model predicts, above means more.
def test_statistic(df):
    E = df["number_set"].astype(str).str.split(",", expand=True).apply(pd.to_numeric, errors="coerce").to_numpy(float)
    t = df["target"].astype(int).to_numpy()
    y = df["rating"].astype(float).to_numpy()
    pad = np.isnan(E)
    n = (~pad).sum(axis=1)
    in_set = (E == t[:, None]).any(axis=1)
    def rate(mask):
        return float(y[mask].mean()) if mask.any() else 0.0
    m_sel = np.zeros(len(t))
    for m in [3, 7, 9, 11]:
        ok = ((E % m == 0) | pad).all(axis=1)
        m_sel = np.where(ok, m, m_sel)
    all_even = ((E % 2 == 0) | pad).all(axis=1)
    all_five = ((E % 5 == 0) | pad).all(axis=1)
    base = (n >= 2) & (m_sel > 0) & ~all_even & ~all_five & ~in_set
    inrule = (t % np.where(m_sel > 0, m_sel, 1)) == 0
    return rate(base & inrule) - rate(base & ~inrule)

results.name: shared_final_digit_match_yes
results.description: In sets of >=2 examples that all end in the same digit (excluding 0 and 5, which are multiples-of-5/10 sets), yes rate for non-example targets ending in that digit; observed below null means people use the shared-final-digit rule less than the model predicts, above means more.
results.code:
# name: shared_final_digit_match_yes
# description: In sets of >=2 examples that all end in the same digit (excluding 0 and 5, which are multiples-of-5/10 sets), yes rate for non-example targets ending in that digit; observed below null means people use the shared-final-digit rule less than the model predicts, above means more.
def test_statistic(df):
    E = df["number_set"].astype(str).str.split(",", expand=True).apply(pd.to_numeric, errors="coerce").to_numpy(float)
    t = df["target"].astype(int).to_numpy()
    y = df["rating"].astype(float).to_numpy()
    pad = np.isnan(E)
    n = (~pad).sum(axis=1)
    in_set = (E == t[:, None]).any(axis=1)
    def rate(mask):
        return float(y[mask].mean()) if mask.any() else 0.0
    d = E % 10
    same = ((d == d[:, :1]) | pad).all(axis=1) & (n >= 2) & (d[:, 0] != 0) & (d[:, 0] != 5)
    return rate(same & (t % 10 == d[:, 0]) & ~in_set)

results.name: mixed_four_example_range_gap
results.description: In 4-example sets mixing odd and even numbers, yes rate for non-example targets inside [min,max] of the examples minus targets outside it; observed above null means people generalize by numerical range in rule-less sets more sharply than the model predicts.
results.code:
# name: mixed_four_example_range_gap
# description: In 4-example sets mixing odd and even numbers, yes rate for non-example targets inside [min,max] of the examples minus targets outside it; observed above null means people generalize by numerical range in rule-less sets more sharply than the model predicts.
def test_statistic(df):
    E = df["number_set"].astype(str).str.split(",", expand=True).apply(pd.to_numeric, errors="coerce").to_numpy(float)
    t = df["target"].astype(int).to_numpy()
    y = df["rating"].astype(float).to_numpy()
    pad = np.isnan(E)
    n = (~pad).sum(axis=1)
    in_set = (E == t[:, None]).any(axis=1)
    def rate(mask):
        return float(y[mask].mean()) if mask.any() else 0.0
    odd = ((E % 2 == 1) & ~pad).any(axis=1)
    even = ((E % 2 == 0) & ~pad).any(axis=1)
    lo, hi = np.nanmin(E, axis=1), np.nanmax(E, axis=1)
    base = (n == 4) & odd & even & ~in_set
    inside = (t >= lo) & (t <= hi)
    return rate(base & inside) - rate(base & ~inside)
